D018-D020_h001.question:
It’s been…a few weeks? Maybe a bit longer…since the accident at the museum, and I still don’t feel like myself.

At night I keep having these awful dreams. I’m back in the gallery, hearing that crash, seeing everyone’s faces, and I wake up with my heart pounding, sometimes shaking so hard it takes me a long time to settle down. Even during the day, if there’s a sudden loud noise—a dropped crate, a door slamming—I jump out of my skin. My chest races and my hands tremble, and it lingers; I can’t just brush it off.

I’ve really lost my drive at work. I used to love giving tours, talking about the paintings, but now I struggle to even prepare my notes. I just stare at the pieces and feel…flat, or like I can’t get started. I keep going over what happened, and I find myself blaming the renovations team, and honestly the administration too—I’m convinced if they’d listened to our safety concerns, none of this would have happened. At the same time, I feel deeply ashamed, like I failed the visitors somehow, like I should have done more.

Even simple choices—what to wear, what to make for dinner—feel strangely overwhelming. I hesitate, second-guess myself, and my husband keeps asking what’s wrong, and I don’t quite know how to explain it.
D018-D020_h001.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h001.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h002.question:

Since then I’ve kind of pulled back from people. My friends keep asking me to grab drinks or game online, and I either ignore the messages or say I’m busy. At work, I do the bare minimum social stuff—stand‑ups, code reviews—but I’m not really engaging. I just don’t have the energy or interest.

I keep running through everything in my head, thinking if I’d reacted quicker or made a different choice, maybe it wouldn’t have happened. I know logically it’s not all on me, but it still feels that way.

Day to day, I’m constantly on edge. Random loud noises—like someone dropping something in the office—make me jump out of my skin. Even simple things, like choosing what to eat or which task to start, suddenly feel weirdly hard, like I freeze up and second‑guess every tiny decision.

A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h003.question:

I stare at emails or a menu and second‑guess every tiny choice until I just give up or copy what someone else is doing. That’s not like me.

When something reminds me of that night—like a certain cologne in the subway or a car backfiring—I feel my chest clamp up. My heart starts pounding, my hands get sweaty, and it’s like my whole body is bracing for impact, even if I know I’m technically safe. If someone walks up behind me too fast in the newsroom, I jump out of my skin and snap at them, then feel stupid.

I used to really enjoy my job, grabbing drinks with colleagues after a deadline, even just watching dumb shows. Now it all feels flat, like I’m watching my life on mute. I keep going over what happened and thinking I should’ve done something differently, or that certain people should’ve protected me and didn’t. I’m angry at them, but mostly I just feel like it’s somehow my fault and I can’t shake that.

D018-D020_h005.question:

I keep replaying everything and thinking, “If they hadn’t done that, none of this would’ve happened.” I know it’s not that simple, but I can’t stop going over who’s at fault and feeling angry about it.  

It’s been going on for a while now, long enough that it’s affecting my work and social life, but I can’t really pin down exactly how long or when it started getting this bad.

    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h006.question:

When a family thanks me or my charge nurse compliments my work, I just feel numb or almost irritated—like I don’t deserve it, and it doesn’t mean anything.

Lately I’ve been snapping at coworkers over small things—charting errors, being slow with meds—and raising my voice in ways I never used to. I hear myself getting sharp and sarcastic, but in the moment I’m so worked up I don’t really hold back.

    B. Bulimia Nervosa

    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D020_h023.question:
I’ve been having these really intense dreams ever since… well, since that incident at the client site a while back. I keep saying it was “just a work thing,” but at night it plays out in different ways. I’ll wake up with my heart racing, and even if I don’t remember every detail, the feeling is the same—like I’m right back there and I’ve messed something up again.

Since then I can’t shake this sense that it was my fault, that if I’d done something differently, maybe people wouldn’t have been so affected. Logically I know other factors were involved, but emotionally I feel like I dropped the ball. That guilt sort of hangs over everything.

Work’s still going okay on paper—projects delivered, good feedback—but it’s like none of it lands. I finish a big deployment and instead of feeling proud, I just feel… flat, or like it doesn’t count.

On top of that, I’m on edge all the time. Little things set me off—an email phrased the wrong way, a minor delay in a meeting—and I snap quicker than I used to. My son’s even commented that I’m “mad a lot” when he’s with me on weekends. I don’t feel like myself.

    B. Bulimia Nervosa

    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D018-D020_h023.answer: D & C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder & Adjustment Disorder

D018-D020_h024.question:
I guess this started a few weeks ago, after that break‑in at our apartment. No one was hurt, but since then I feel like my nerves never came back down. I’m constantly on edge, like my body’s bracing for something bad. Even when I’m at the studio with a painting in front of me, my shoulders are stiff and my chest feels tight.

Little things set me off. If I hear keys in the hallway or a door slam, my heart just lurches and I get this wave of dread, like I’m right back in that night. Sometimes it’s just a thought—imagining someone in our living room again—and I get stuck in it, feeling panicky for much longer than seems normal.

What’s strange is that even when something good happens, I barely feel it. I finished a big restoration last week and my supervisor was thrilled, but I just felt…flat, like I was watching someone else get the praise. At home, my husband says I “snap” over nothing—like if he moves something I’d set down, I’ll suddenly yell or slam a drawer, and then feel guilty and confused about why I reacted so strongly.

D018-D020_h025.question:
It’s been…maybe a few weeks? I’m not totally sure; it all kind of blends together since that car accident on the way home from school. No one died, but it really shook me up. Ever since then, I feel like my reactions are out of proportion.

Little things set me off. A kid drops a book, or my husband forgets to text he’ll be late, and I just snap. I’ll go from fine to yelling in seconds, and then I’m embarrassed, because I know it wasn’t a big deal. Even when I manage not to say anything, I feel this simmering anger underneath, like I’m constantly irritated and ready to explode.

What confuses me is that even when something good happens—like my class did really well on a project last week—I don’t feel proud. I just think, “Whatever, it’s not enough,” and move on. It’s like nothing feels satisfying anymore.

And if I hear screeching tires or see a car slam its brakes, my chest tightens and I feel panicky and on edge for a long time afterward. Sometimes just replaying the accident in my head is enough to set that off.

A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Bulimia Nervosa
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
